claims.text: Traditional casting or slow-sintering routes produce boride-based components with relatively high porosity.
Traditional casting or slow-sintering routes produce less-continuous protective phases.
Rapid-sintering powder metallurgy will densify the boride-based component and reduce its porosity.
Rapid sintering will promote a continuous, more uniform boron-rich phase at the component surface.
Reduced porosity decreases pathways for molten-aluminum infiltration.
A continuous boron-rich surface phase acts as a chemical barrier to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Reduced infiltration and the boron-rich chemical barrier slow penetration of corrosive species.
Rapid-sintered components will exhibit approximately 20–30% better molten-aluminum corrosion resistance than conventionally cast or slow-sintered components.
The improvement should remain effective under molten-aluminum exposure conditions typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating operations.
Maintaining the integrity of the boride phase is necessary for the predicted corrosion improvement.
Overly rapid sintering may induce unwanted phase transformations or residual stresses.
Unwanted phase transformations or residual stresses may negate the corrosion-resistance benefit.
